s15.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:30 PM → 9:50 PM · MID-CITY — THE LONG WAY ROUND
body: The supper place is a corner bar on Bienville with a kitchen in the back and a Barq’s sign in the window that has lost the bottom of its *s*. Inside it’s one long room under a pressed-tin ceiling painted so many times the pattern has gone soft as cake frosting: the bar down one wall with a television over the end of it, six tables down the other in red oilcloth, and by the bathroom door a jukebox with its colors going round. Two men in Entergy jackets are at the bar with their elbows either side of their beers. At the far end of it a woman in a Saints sweatshirt is doing the *Picayune* crossword in pen.

Lena doesn’t give him a menu. She gives the man behind the bar the order from across the room, a whole muffuletta, warm, and two Barq’s in the bottle, and when it comes out on butcher paper she cuts it in four with the bread knife that comes with it and takes the biggest quarter, and puts the second-biggest in front of him, which he understands to be manners. It’s the size of a hubcap, round bread with sesame on top and the oil off the olive salad soaked clean through the bottom, ham and salami and mortadella and provolone gone soft in the heat. Nonna would have opinions about olives on a sandwich, all of them in Italian, and would eat two quarters.
“Well?” Lena says.
“I’m from Youngstown. We don’t say anything till the second quarter.”
“That *is* your second quarter.”
He looks down at his paper. It is. “It’s good,” he says, with his mouth full, and she nods as though she cooked it.

Over the bar the television has the news on with the sound off. The parade again, from a helicopter, Canal Street black with people from one side to the other under the lights; a man at a desk with a stack of papers he doesn’t look at. Then, across the bottom of the screen in white letters beside the five rings: VANCOUVER 2010, and a count of days to go, which is two. Lena looks up at it with her quarter halfway to her mouth. Jack looks up at it too. It goes to the weather, a map of the Gulf with nothing on it, clear and cold up to the lake, and she takes her bite.

While she’s buttoning the jean jacket at the door, somebody at the bar feeds the jukebox, and the Neville Brothers come on, slow, Aaron’s voice going up into the tin ceiling, higher than a man’s voice has any business going, and the two men in the Entergy jackets quit talking to let it.
Outside she turns left. Dupre Street is to the right: five days in this city and he knows that much. She doesn’t explain, and he goes left with her.

It’s full dark and cold, and there are more stars out over the rooflines than Glenwood Avenue gets all February. The side streets back here are narrow and quiet, the houses close up to the sidewalk on their piers, shotguns and doubles and a camelback here and there, a porch light on every third one. He starts to see the lines, and once he’s seen one he can’t stop. On most of the houses it’s gone under new paint, and you’d only know it was there because the paint below the porch rail is a shade brighter than the paint above, like a wall where a picture used to hang. On some it’s been left. A yellow double with green shutters wears it on purpose, a brown stripe straight across the front at the height of a man’s chest, and somebody has lettered under it, small and neat in white, *8·29·05*, and hung the flower boxes right below that, full of pansies. Two doors down there’s a line with a fainter line a foot under it, where the water stood a week, and went down a foot, and stood again.
Somewhere after the yellow double her hand has come through his arm, and her shoulder is against his, and they walk like that.

Halfway down the next block there is a house nobody came back to. The windows are plywood gone gray. The porch roof sags in the middle like a hammock, and grass has come up through the treads of the steps. By the front door, on the siding, is a big X in orange spray paint gone pale with weather, with something written into each of its four corners: a date at the top, letters on one side, letters on the other, which he can’t read and she doesn’t read for him. In the bottom corner there is a 0.
Lena stops on the sidewalk in front of it.
“Zero’s the good number,” she says.
She walks on, and he walks with her.
At the next corner he looks back over his shoulder, toward the bayou. “It came from there?”

“Everybody thinks the bayou.” She takes her hand back out of his arm and turns him by the sleeve to face the other way, up the dark street toward the lake, where there’s nothing to see but a streetlight and a cat crossing under it. “The canals. Seventeenth Street. London Avenue. The walls gave out, and this city’s tipped toward the lake like Mémère’s kitchen floor: drop a pea by the stove and it ends up at the back door. So it came in at the low end and filled from there, like a sink, till it got all the way up to us.” She lets go of his sleeve. “Wes could tell you to the inch. He’s going to build the walls right.”
“Good,” Jack says.

She wants Youngstown, block by block, and he tells it. The lines there aren’t water. You can tell the year a street gave up by its paint. Out along the river where the Sheet & Tube was there’s a stretch of chain-link with a gate in it and nothing behind the gate but sumac, and every time Pop drives Nonna past it she makes him slow the truck down, and crosses herself.
“For the mill,” Lena says.

“For my grandfather. To her it’s the same thing.” Sunday gravy at two. Not two-oh-five. At two-oh-five Nonna has said grace without you, and you say it again standing up, by yourself, with the table watching and Gina timing you on the microwave clock.
“That’s Mémère with the rosary. You come in on the third decade, you start over from the Creed, with her counting.”

body.text: He tells her about Rosie’s dinosaur, the green one from the gift shop at Cabazon, riding home to Glenwood Avenue in his duffel, and the name on the box they took away, and that Jude knows, and isn’t telling, and Rosie can’t ever. Lena hears him out with her hands in her jacket.
“Then she doesn’t hear it from me.” She spits in her palm, neatly, the way Mémère does business with the man who sells her satsumas, and holds it out, and he shakes on it.
He tells her Jude asked him whether Ohio has dinosaurs.
She shakes her head at the sidewalk. “That boy’s going to think about that till Easter.”

body: “How’s Danny?”
“He said watch the game. All of it.”
“Did you?”
“All of it.”
She nods. A little farther on she asks what he’s giving Hale.
“You first.”
“The bag.”
“Four thousand words on a Schwegmann’s bag.”
“On penance. In a bag. He said nothing about football. He didn’t say one word about bags.” She looks up at him. “You?”
“The second line.”
“You haven’t been in one.”
“Not yet.”

body.else: “Then you owe me a second line.”

body: A block on, under a streetlight, she says, “Laney’s been crossing herself. She’s *Baptist*.”
“Theo gave Kevin his phone.”
Lena stops dead under the light. “Lord. What did they *do*?”
“I was going to ask you.”

She looks at him, and he looks at her, and they have nothing, either of them, and she takes his arm again and they go on. At the corner she turns left again. A block after that they pass a corner store with burglar bars and a hand-lettered sign in the window for hot boudin, and he would swear on Nonna’s gravy that they passed it an hour ago, from the other side.

choices.text: “This isn’t the way to the house.”
response: “This isn’t the way to the house,” he says.

She doesn’t change it. She takes them two more blocks wrong and one back, under a wire with a pair of sneakers hung over it by the laces, and at last round onto Dupre Street, where halfway down the block every window in her mother’s house is lit.
She looks at him sideways, under the burglar bars. “Juan Diego was in a hurry.”

She walks on with her hand through his arm. It’s three more blocks, all of them the wrong way, before they come round the last corner onto Dupre Street and see the house down the block with its porch light on and the Odyssey at the curb.
He doesn’t say anything. They walk.

The sidewalks back here are broken into slabs by the roots, heaved up and tipped every which way, and she knows where every one of them is and steps over it with her eyes on the street, and by the second block he has learned them too. When they turn onto Dupre Street at last the house is lit from end to end, down the block, the Odyssey dark at the curb in front of it.

s16.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:05 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE SIDE YARD — THE LINE
body: They don’t go up the steps. Lena goes past the foot of them and in at the gate in the chain-link along the side of the lot, by the trash cans, and holds it for him, and as he comes round the corner of the house the porch is above them, lit.

Theo is in Tony’s kitchen chair, the one that lives out there, in the good coat with the collar up. Tony is beside him on the swing in a Saints windbreaker with a cup of chicory going cold on his knee. The transistor sits on the rail on its coat-hanger antenna, playing WWL low, a man calling in from Chalmette about the parade and the host agreeing with every word of it, and Tony has the radio turned square to his face. The two of them are just sitting. Behind them, in the front window, the curtain is held back by one finger, and the face beside the finger is Laney’s, with Mémère’s lamp on behind her.
All three of them look at Jack and Lena coming up the side yard. Then all three look away at once: Theo at the street, Tony at the radio, and the curtain falling shut.

body.text: The kitchen window throws a yellow square across the grass to the back of the lot. Lena walks into it and out the far side of it to the shed, and puts her back to the boards, against the line he has had his hand on.
body.else: The kitchen window throws a yellow square across the grass to the back of the lot. Lena walks into it and out the far side of it to the shed, and puts her back to the boards, against the line she showed him with her phone.

body: She leans there in Remy’s sweatshirt and the jean jacket, at the edge of the light, and the line crosses her at the collarbone. The medal he fastened at four o’clock lies on it, outside the collar of the sweatshirt, on its mended chain, and catches the window.

He stands in front of her. Up close her face is still pink from the wind off the bayou, and there’s a fleck of gold at her hairline, left from Tuesday’s fleur-de-lis, that two washings haven’t found. She has been talking for three hours, and now she isn’t. The cold is coming up out of the grass into his boots. On the porch the man from Chalmette is laughing at something on the telephone, and two yards over a dog is having its say about it, and the house behind him is going quiet for the night, room by room.
Her hand comes up out of her jacket pocket and lies flat across his chest, over the Carhartt, at the height the line would be on him.
“Here,” she says.

She leaves it there. Her palm is cold through the canvas, and then it isn’t. His heart is going under it hard enough that she has to feel it, and there’s nothing in the world he can do about that. He wants her. Standing in a dark yard with her back to the shed and her grandmother’s medal on the waterline, he wants her so much it is very nearly simple, and his hands stay in his pockets. They’ve been there the length of Mid-City. She looks up at him in the yellow light, and doesn’t move her hand.

choices.key: By the shed on Dupre Street, with the old waterline across the boards and her medal on it, Lena put her hand on your chest where the line would be. You said: I’m here.
response: Her hand doesn’t move for a long time. On the porch the radio goes to a commercial for a mattress store and comes back. Her fingers close on the canvas, a fistful of the Carhartt, and hold it, and let it go, and then her hand comes off his chest and back into her pocket, and the cold comes in where it was.

choices.text: *Put your hand over hers and keep it there.*
choices.key: By the shed on Dupre Street Lena put her hand on your chest where the waterline would be. You put your hand over hers and kept it there.
response: He takes his right hand out of his pocket and puts it over hers, and keeps it there. Her hand is under his and his heart is under hers, and the kitchen light is on them both, and on the line behind her, and on the medal.
When she takes her hand back she slides it out from under his slowly, a knuckle at a time, and his hand is left on his own coat where hers was.

choices.text: “Your father said he wanted the steps steep.”
choices.key: By the shed on Dupre Street Lena put her hand on your chest where the waterline would be. You said her father wanted the steps steep. If you can carry it up those steps, you keep it, she said.
response: “Your father said he wanted the steps steep.”

She looks at him over her own wrist, in the yellow light, with her back to the line. “Daddy says if you can carry it up those steps, you keep it.” Her hand stays where it is until she’s finished saying it, and then it comes down off his chest and goes into her pocket with the other one.

s16a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:15 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE SIDE YARD — TAG
body: When she goes, it’s round the back corner of the house to the kitchen door, and not past him.

She goes up the back steps. At the top she puts her hand on the frame of the screen door and stands there with it half open, in the light, with her back to the yard. Then she’s through it. The spring brings the screen door to behind her, and a moment later the kitchen light goes off, and the yellow square goes off the grass.

The side yard is dark. The big boil pot is upside down on the picnic table where somebody put it to drain on Sunday, a dull round shape against the fence. On the porch the radio goes off in the middle of the man from Chalmette. The kitchen chair scrapes on the boards, and Theo says something to Tony, low, that Jack doesn’t catch, and Tony laughs, a big short bark of a laugh, and the front screen door goes. Up in the attic gable the window over the box fan is dark.
From somewhere over the back fence comes sweet olive, which he couldn’t have named on Saturday.
The RAZR is in the inside pocket of the Carhartt and it doesn’t make a sound. In Burnaby they’re shooting all night. Tonight’s the moon: that’s the rule, and under the rule he isn’t allowed to worry.

body.text: He says the words off the medal once more, under his breath, to the back of the shed. *O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.*

body: He stays out in the yard with his hands in his pockets and his breath going up. In front of him the line runs the length of the boards in the dark. He can’t see it. He doesn’t need to.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I told her that’s what I meant in San Francisco: she as good as told me to. She says she said no such thing — that I’m lying to win an argument about a book. I was on the other end of that phone. I said it was the night for calling people liars, and got the date wrong, and she had the date. Then we said things we’ve never said. I told her she can’t forgive a status. She asked me if I still go up. Hale stood up and stopped it; the dog felt it through the floor. On her way out she told Hale Sarah let him believe he’d been replaced. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney. Friday in the lounge Laney found the taco picture. Lena laughed. Then she saw me. Then she read the rest of the screen and shut the laptop. Monday at the seminar she sat at the far end, and Hale kept her after with the door shut. Candlemas she carried a candle in the procession. Wednesday morning in the lobby she had a legal pad and a trip — New Orleans, Kevin’s mother’s van, her mother’s house — and she said to Theo, not to me, that her daddy says bring the Ohio boy. She was only telling him what he said. It’s not my trip. Thursday night we packed Kevin’s mother’s van without a word to each other. Everything went through Kevin and Laney. She asked Kevin for the way-back; she got it. She wrote WHO DAT · 3 DAYS on the back glass. Friday at five Skye told her to win her game. Safe flight, she said. She rode to the Rincon with her hood up. Friday in Kevin’s mother’s van, past Picacho, she said one thing to me — that I always did read a margin well — and from Tucson to New Mexico we had the worst fight we’ve ever had, in front of everybody. I said the thing about the movie called *Jack*. She didn’t say anything after that. At three in the morning, short of Van Horn, she said, Quarter tank. She bought two coffees. We talked about nothing till Balmorhea, and she fell asleep. At Fort Stockton neither of us said anything about it. Saturday in San Antonio she asked if Hale’s copy is any good. Hers is better. At the Basin she said she asked Kevin for the way-back so she wouldn’t have to look at me. Saturday night on Dupre Street I carried her up her mother’s steps, asleep. At the table she pulled me down next to her. The shed out back has a line on it at four and a half feet. Sunday at the eight o’clock at Holy Rosary her mother put me in the pew between her and her grandmother. She was behind me in the line when I went up. Her grandmother put the two of us on the floor for the game, in front, where she could see us. At the onside kick she put her face in my shoulder. When it was over she came off the curb, and I caught her, in the middle of Dupre Street. At a quarter to four in the morning on Esplanade she fell asleep against me. She said she wanted me here for this. Since September. Monday she ate the toast off my plate and read me the box score. Tuesday she painted a fleur-de-lis on my face and stood inside my coat on Canal for most of the parade. Wednesday she took me to her grandmother’s tomb and told her the score, and the clasp of her medal had broken in the crowd, and she had me fasten it. On the bridge over the bayou she argued Scholastica’s side and looked at the sky. Well, she said. I didn’t ask.
